children: Ask anyone about India’s relationship with gold, and the conversation usually turns to grand weddings, festive buying during Dhanteras, or family vaults passed down through generations. It is a familiar story: India as a voracious consumer, absorbing around 700 to 800 tonnes of physical gold every year. According to World Gold Council data, India accounts for nearly 15 per cent of total global gold demand (768 tonnes) and roughly 28 per cent of global jewellery demand (430.5 tonnes).

Yet, treating India merely as a giant sink for the world’s precious metals misses the real story. India holds little to no domestic gold mines of its own. Its true global influence stems not from pulling ore out of the ground, but from what happens after imported bullion arrives at its ports.

India’s annual gold import bill often hovers around the $59 billion mark, making bullion one of the largest components of the nation’s import balance alongside crude oil. Rather than viewing this outflow simply as an economic cost, the industry treats raw gold as a vital input for a massive, export-focused manufacturing engine.

The country’s provisional gems and jewellery exports reached approximately $27.71 billion in FY2026. This trade spans cut and polished diamonds, intricate gold and silver jewellery, and lab-grown gemstones. In fact, India processes over 90 per cent of the world’s cut and polished diamonds by volume, representing roughly a quarter of global diamond exports.

Picture the journey of a single piece of Kundan or Polki jewellery in Jaipur. In a workshop off the lanes of Johari Bazaar, a master karigar sets gemstones in pure gold foil using hand techniques passed down through generations of Rajasthani craft families. A few decades ago, that artisan relied entirely on hand tools and trained judgement to gauge metal purity.

Today, the same craftsman works alongside laser soldering systems, XRF testing equipment and 3D wax printers. Across Rajasthan, from the old-city workshops of to the organised manufacturing units, the state’s signature traditions of Kundan, Polki and Meenakari are being paired with computerised design systems. Technology is not replacing the human touch; it is giving Rajasthan’s traditional artisans the speed and precision needed to meet strict international standards.

As modern consumers demand ethical supply chains and verified provenance, the global jewellery trade is undergoing a structural shift. It is no longer enough to offer a beautifully finished ring; buyers want to know where the gold was refined, whether it carries ESG credibility, and if the diamonds were ethically sourced. Indian manufacturers are actively adopting digital traceability tools, blockchain verification, and international quality certifications. This moves the industry beyond mere compliance, turning responsible sourcing into a core selling point.

At the same time, the industry is shifting its ambitions from backend contract manufacturing to front-end brand building. For decades, Indian facilities have crafted exquisite pieces sold under European and American luxury labels. The next logical step is building home-grown Indian houses with global retail footprints, capturing the higher margins associated with brand equity, design IP, and direct customer relationships.

India’s strength in the global market does not lie in owning vast gold reserves or running deep underground mines. Its true competitive advantage comes from an unmatched ability to refine, cut, design, and add value to every gram of metal that enters its borders. The long-term trajectory of India’s gems and jewellery trade will not be measured simply by how many tonnes of gold its domestic market consumes. The real metric of success is how efficiently the country transforms imported raw materials into high-margin, tech-enabled, globally recognised luxury products.
(The author is Chairman and Managing Director,

title: From gold consumer to global powerhouse: How India refines, designs, and dominates
